newsitem.title: GUINEA: Guinea lawyers oppose state security court.
newsitem.headline: Guinea lawyers oppose state security court.

text.p: Lawyers in the West African state of Guinea have publicly denounced a government plan to use a special state security court to try soldiers who staged a 1996 mutiny.

The lawyers guild, in a statement agreed on July 16, said that a June 28 decree nominating members of the court threatened the independence of the judiciary and urged President Lansana Conte to think again.
The guild argued that the 1990 multi-party constitution made special courts unlawful.
"Common law crimes committed by the soldiers and paramilitary personnel come under the jurisdiction of the judicial courts," it said, quoting a 1988 law.
Mutineers shelled and destroyed Conte's presidential palace during the 1996 pay revolt. Conteh, forced to hide, said at the time that forces behind the revolt were trying to topple him.
Speculation that the soldiers will be put on trial has heightened tension in the capital Conakry, visitors say.
The government freed more than 60 mutiny suspects last August. Officials at the time said a small group of officers remained in detention and would stand trial.
The state security court was set up in 1985 to try people implicated in a failed coup plot that year.

The lawyers said that under new laws the appeal court should hear cases against the 1996 mutineers. The handling of the case had breached existing laws and guidelines, stripping lawyers of the power to represent defendants properly, they added.
They recalled the constitution enshrined the independence of the judiciary from the executive and legislative authorities.
Conte seized power in 1984. He won a disputed 1993 presidential election.
